newsitem.title: CONGO: Power play and ethnic rivalry in Congo Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Power play and ethnic rivalry in Congo Brazzaville.

text.p: Shortly after Laurent Kabila toppled Zaire's veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko across the river, a senior Western diplomat described the former French colony of Congo as "an oasis of peace in the middle of a turbulent ocean".

True, the Congo Brazzaville economy, rich in oil yet burdened by debt, had shown signs of picking up -- 6.8 percent real growth in 1996 after just 0.9 percent in 1995 and minus 5.5 percent the year before.

But barely a month later, undercurrents of ethnic tension that had been bubbling away since the slaughter of at least 2,000 people in political and ethnic clashes in the capital Brazzaville in 1993 and early 1994, boiled over again.

"There are three armed factions. Everything points to the idea that if there's one man who isn't pleased, he won't hesitate to resort to arms," one U.N. regional security adviser said before the storm broke.
In 1993, the clashes followed disputed parliamentary elections. Colourfully named militias -- Cobras, Ninjas or Zulus -- slugged it out in the southern suburbs.
This time, manoeuvring ahead of a July 27 presidential election seems to be the trigger. The militias, supposedly disbanded and merged into the armed forces, are back.
President Pascal Lissouba, a civilian elected in 1992, accuses former Marxist president Denis Sassou Nguesso and his Cobras, of trying to stage a coup.

Sassou Nguesso, a military strongman who was president from 1979 until voted out of office in a 1992 democratic transition, accuses Lissouba and his allies of fomenting violence to force the postponement of the July election.

"The fighting is intensely tribal... When they get a chance they massacre each other's tribes indiscriminately," one Western diplomatic source said of the latest showdown. "The heavy weaponry that is being used, particularly multiple rocket launchers, must be causing very heavy civilian casualties."
But the roots of the crisis have as much to do with power as ethnicity.

Sassou Nguesso, having seen fellow one-time Marxist Mathieu Kerekou return to power through the ballot box in tiny Benin in 1996, returned home in January from over a year in France and launched an undeclared campaign for the presidency.

A cross-section of sources say that militia from Sassou-Nguesso's Mboshi tribe have been in the thick of the fray fighting soldiers loyal to Lissouba and militia from former president Jacques-Joachim Yhombi-Opango's Kouyou ethnic group.
Yhombi-Opango is Lissouba's campaign manager. Lissouba comes from the minority Nzabi tribe.
The showdown erupted into firefights on June 5.
Lissouba's government, cracking down on private militias and illegal possession of firearms, surrounded Sassou Nguesso's house to arrest members of his entourage on murder charges.
The move followed clashes in the north between Sassou Nguesso and Yhombi-Opango supporters, which killed 16 people.
The Brazzaville death toll this time round is unknown because foreign military and aid workers cannot reach many areas under fire. Witnesses and residents say looting has been rife.
The capital's mayor, Bernard Kolelas, who is from the Brazzaville-centred Kongo ethnic group and whose Ninjas were in the thick of fighting in 1993, has kept out of the latest fray.
Runner up to Lissouba in 1992, he has taken on the role of mediator -- winning Lissouba's backing for dialogue.
Countries across Central Africa have a rich but volatile ethnic mix -- a legacy inherited with colonial boundaries.

Events in Brazzaville bear a striking ressemblance to events in Bangui, capital of neighbouring Central African Republic, where three army mutinies in under a year spilled over into ethnic bloodletting.
Northern supporters of President Ange-Felix Patasse fought southern Yakoma, the tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba.
French troops moved in as a buffer, and, after mediation launched by the Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso in Decmber, quickly handed over to an African peacekeeping force.
France has reinforced its troops in Brazzaville -- they went there to help evacuate foreign nationals from Kinshasa in the event of a bloodbath there but were never needed.

But French commanders say they are there to protect or evacuate the 2,000-strong French community and other foreign nationals. Despite the death of one French soldier on Saturday, they say they have no plans to intervene directly.
Over the years, a string of African ideologues have argued that because of ethnic rivalries, multi-party politics may not be the best model for African democracy.
Across the River Congo, Kabila has banned the activity of political parties in his Democratic Republic of Congo and has promised elections for April 1999.

Uganda's president, Yoweri Musevi, one of Kabila's mentors, does very well mixing free-market reforms with an absence of party politics. Kabila has yet to say whether his promised elections will be multi-party or not.
In the meantime, the fate of Congo's July 27 poll is far from clear.
